analysis.one_liner: Strips monopoly exclusivity from orphan drugs whose makers can recover costs within 12 years of sales.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 402-23 in May 2021 after an earlier attempt failed 250-168, but the Senate never acted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a drug treats a rare disease and its maker says it can't make the money back, the FDA grants a seven-year monopoly on the U.S. market. This bill says that protection can only be granted, or kept, if the maker truly can't recover its development costs within the first 12 years of U.S. sales — counting all of its drugs sold under the same rare-disease designation. It would apply to monopolies already granted, giving companies 60 days to prove they qualify or lose the protection.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with rare diseases, who often face very high prices for drugs with no competition. By shortening or denying monopoly periods for drugs whose makers can actually recover their costs, the bill would let competing versions reach the market sooner and put downward pressure on prices. Insurers and government health programs that pay for these drugs would also spend less.

how_it_helps.text: For drugs designated as orphan drugs on the ground that they are not economically viable, the FDA may grant the seven-year market exclusivity period only if the sponsor shows no reasonable expectation of recovering development and availability costs within the first 12 years of U.S. sales.

In making that judgment, the FDA must count sales from all of a sponsor's drugs covered by the same rare-disease designation, closing the route of splitting one drug among several designations to preserve monopoly protection.
The requirement applies retroactively: a sponsor with exclusivity already granted must demonstrate it qualifies within 60 days of enactment or the FDA must revoke the exclusivity.

analysis.who_pays: Orphan-drug manufacturers, chiefly those designated under the economic-viability criterion, would lose or face earlier loss of seven-year monopoly protection — both on drugs in the pipeline and, retroactively, on drugs already on the market. The standard good-faith objection is that market exclusivity is the main incentive for developing drugs for diseases that affect very few people, so shrinking it could mean fewer rare-disease medicines get developed. Applying the rule retroactively also changes the terms after companies made investment decisions.

drawbacks.text: Market exclusivity exists precisely because rare-disease drugs are often not profitable on their own; restricting it could reduce the incentive to develop treatments for very small patient populations, a tradeoff an honest supporter has to acknowledge.
The bill applies retroactively, revoking exclusivity already granted unless sponsors qualify within 60 days of enactment, changing the rules after approval and investment decisions were made.
The scope is narrow: it only reaches drugs designated under the rare-disease economic-viability criterion, so most orphan drugs and their monopoly periods are untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific gap — drugs that got monopoly protection as 'not economically viable' even though their makers could recover costs, especially by aggregating sales across multiple designations — while leaving the incentive intact for genuinely unprofitable drugs through the 12-year recovery test. The main real cost is the risk of weaker development incentives for ultra-rare diseases and the disruption of retroactive revocations. On balance it is a targeted consumer-price measure rather than a sweeping attack on the orphan-drug incentive system, and the House's near-unanimous final vote suggests even its skeptics saw it that way once given a normal vote.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 402-23 after an initial two-thirds vote failed, but the Senate sent it to its health committee, which never brought it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Madeleine Dean introduced the bill on March 8, 2021, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Budget Committees.

A first attempt to pass it under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority — failed 250-168, with all 214 voting Democrats in favor and 168 voting Republicans opposed.
After the Rules Committee reported a rule providing closed-rule consideration, the House passed the bill on May 19, 2021, 402-23, with all 215 voting Democrats and 187 voting Republicans in favor.

The Senate received the bill on May 20, 2021, and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Orphan-drug manufacturers came out ahead: they kept their existing exclusivity and faced no new limits, while rare-disease patients continued to face limited competition and the prices that come with it.

sides.party_line_note: The first vote split by party — 214 of 218 voting Democrats for, 168 of 204 voting Republicans against, failing 250-168 — but when leaders brought the bill back under a rule, it passed 402-23 with only 23 Republicans opposed and no Democrats.

industries.note: The bill revokes or denies seven-year market exclusivity for drugs designated on economic-viability grounds whenever the sponsor can recover development costs within 12 years of U.S. sales, counting all same-designation drugs. That monopoly protection is what keeps competing versions off the market and rare-disease drug prices high.
Shorter or absent exclusivity means earlier opportunity to compete for drugs that would otherwise be locked up for seven years.

industries.industry: Health insurers and public drug payers
industries.note: Competition on formerly exclusive orphan drugs would lower what insurers and programs like Medicare pay for them.
